one_liner: A wide-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 1.3x fair value. Interesting below about $27.

profile.what: Bank of America is the second-largest US bank, with about 70 million consumer and small-business clients, the Merrill Lynch wealth business, and a large investment bank.
profile.money: Net interest income from loans and securities funded by its large deposit base is the largest source of profit, so earnings rise with interest rates. Fees come from wealth management, cards, investment banking and trading.
profile.valued: Valued on price to tangible book and P/E. Its multiple has lagged JPMorgan's because it bought long-dated bonds at low yields in 2020-21, which cut returns when rates rose; the discount narrows as those bonds mature.
profile.peer_group: Financials · bank, insurer or asset manager

summary.sentence: A deposit-rich bank whose earnings rise as low-yielding bonds mature.
strengths: Share count down about 5% in a year.
risks: Return on equity is only about 10%.

meaning.what_it_does: The second-largest US bank, with Merrill wealth management.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Net interest income on loans and securities, plus fees.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: One of the largest and cheapest deposit bases in the country.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Credit losses, or losses on long-dated bonds when rates rise.

moat.summary: A national deposit franchise that is very hard to replicate.

industry.summary: Banking changes slowly, but results depend on credit cycles and interest rates.

management.summary: Conservative credit culture since the financial crisis.

valuation.method: Banks are valued on book value, not free cash flow. Justified price-to-book = (ROE − 3% growth) ÷ (required return − 3%), using a normalised ROE of 9.1% (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM, capped at 25%) and a required return of 11% (low) to 9% (high): 0.76–1.02 × book value per share of $43.01.

methods.name: Excess-return model on book value
methods.basis: Book value per share $43.01 × 0.76–1.02. This is how Damodaran values banks and insurers: equity is worth book value plus the returns earned above the cost of equity.
